title: Detect, Decide, Unlearn: A Transfer-Aware Framework for Continual Learning
one_liner: A continual learning system that detects when old knowledge hurts new learning and surgically removes it instead of keeping everything.
lead: Continual learning means a model learns new tasks one after another from a stream of data. Most research tries to keep old knowledge intact to avoid forgetting. But old knowledge can backfire: when a weight learned to solve task A but would make task B worse if kept, freezing it forces task B to learn around a useless constraint, leaving accuracy lower than if the weight were free to adapt. This paper asks: what if we selectively forget weights that hurt new learning?

paras: A student learns to identify cats, then dogs, then birds. If the model keeps all its cat-knowledge locked in place to prevent forgetting, it may freeze patterns that are useless or wrong for bird-recognition. The more tasks learned, the more of these traps accumulate.

A beginner might try: hold weights still (freeze them). But this backfires because many early weights encode task-specific patterns; freezing them forces new tasks to work around useless constraints. The model gets slower and less accurate with each new task, even though it remembers the old ones.

callout.html: Keeping all old knowledge makes new learning worse when old and new tasks interfere with each other.

panels.title: 3. Detecting when old patterns hurt new tasks
panels.viz_args: Conflict detector: old ways push against new ways.
panels.caption: Math identifies weights where old and new learning directions fight.

panels.title: 4. Unlearning outdated weights

steps.text: Before learning a new task, measure which weights face opposite nudging directions from old and new tasks.
Quantify how opposite the learning directions are: if old and new nudges point opposite ways, that weight is in conflict.
For conflicting weights, activate unlearning. For non-conflicting, freeze to protect old knowledge.
Reset conflicting weights to a neutral state, freeing that capacity for new task learning.
Periodically scan the entire model and reset the weakest weights across all tasks to reclaim more capacity.

paras: The paper changes which weights stay frozen and which reset to neutral. Standard continual learning freezes everything to protect old tasks. DEDUCE freezes non-conflicting weights and resets conflicting ones, making space for new learning.
object.object: weights: which ones freeze vs reset

hidden.h2: Gradient conflict: the signal of interference
hidden.name: Gradient conflict magnitude
paras: A gradient is a direction you nudge a weight to fix an error. If the old task's gradient points one way and the new task's gradient points the opposite way, the weight is caught in a tug-of-war. The conflict magnitude measures: how hard are they pulling in opposite directions?

The paper estimates this by computing the gradient of each weight on the old task, then on the new task, and measuring how opposite their directions are. A high conflict means old and new tasks fundamentally disagree on what that weight should do.

heat.caption: Darker weights have higher gradient conflict and will be unlearned.

reads.html: Gradient conflict is the amount that old and new tasks pull a weight in opposite directions.
The paper computes how much old and new learning directions point opposite ways by multiplying their components. If the result is negative, the weight conflicts and unlearning activates.

paras: When two tasks disagree on a weight, trying to satisfy both is impossible. The weight becomes a compromise that makes both tasks worse. By resetting conflicting weights to neutral, the model gives up on that specific compromise, freeing the weight to learn a new pattern that serves the new task.

Non-conflicting weights stay frozen because they encode useful information for the old task that does not hurt the new task. The model learns the new task by using a mixture: some weights (the freed ones) adapt to new patterns, and others (the protected ones) keep old knowledge. This lets the model add new capabilities without erasing old ones.

Periodically, the model also wipes out the weakest weights globally (the ones that have low importance across all tasks learned so far). This reclaims capacity that was never critical, making room for new tasks to grow.

stages.s: Find weights where they point opposite ways
Train the new task with freed weights adapting
New task learned, old task still accurate

math.words: conflict_score = gradient_old dot gradient_new; if negative (pointing opposite), unlearning activates.
math.equation: conflict_i = grad_old_i · grad_new_i; if conflict_i < 0, unlearn weight i
symbols: direction to nudge weight i to fix errors in the old task
direction to nudge weight i to fix errors in the new task
a number measuring how opposite these directions are; negative means pulling apart
a single weight in the model

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Weight w1: old task gradient = (+3.0), new task gradient = (-2.0). Dot product = 3.0 × (-2.0) = -6.0. Negative, so unlearn w1.
Weight w2: old task gradient = (+2.0), new task gradient = (+1.5). Dot product = 2.0 × 1.5 = +3.0. Positive, so freeze w2.
Same weight moved the same amount, but w1 and w2 had opposite signs in their gradients, revealing the conflict.

math.note: A negative dot product means the two tasks pull the weight in opposite directions, so resetting it breaks the tug-of-war.

bars.h2: Accuracy before and after each task

charts.title: Naive freezing (all weights locked)
charts.note: Frozen weights block Task B from learning well. New task starves.

charts.title: DEDUCE (selective unlearning)
charts.note: Unfrozen conflicting weights let Task B learn fast. Non-conflicting weights still protect Task A.

items.b: Resetting too many weights erases useful knowledge.
items.html: If the conflict detector is too sensitive, it unlearns weights that actually did help both tasks, because those weights would have learned useful shared patterns if left alone. The model becomes forgetful. Fix: tune the conflict threshold to be stricter so only truly opposite directions trigger unlearning.

items.b: If old and new tasks do not conflict, nothing is gained.
items.html: Some task sequences have no gradient conflicts. In these cases, freezing works fine, and DEDUCE is unnecessary overhead. Fix: skip unlearning on sequences with no detected conflicts.

items.b: Global unlearning can wipe out weights that suddenly matter.
items.html: Periodically resetting weak weights risks erasing knowledge that becomes important later. Fix: weight the reset decision by how recent each weight was used.
DEDUCE detects true conflicts (old and new gradients genuinely oppose), resets only those weights, and measures importance carefully before global unlearning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a model that learns Task A (classify images into two groups), then Task B (classify images into two different groups, where some patterns from A are useless). Measure: Does freezing all weights (naive) drop accuracy on Task B more than DEDUCE does? Does DEDUCE keep Task A accuracy higher than if we simply reset all weights (the opposite extreme)?
demo.metric_eq: forgetting = accuracy_A_before - accuracy_A_after_learning_B; interference = accuracy_B_with_frozen_weights - accuracy_B_with_DEDUCE; show interference is large and forgetting is small
demo.closing: The demo must show that unlearning conflicting weights recovers Task B accuracy without forgetting Task A, whereas freezing everything causes Task B to stagnate.
